abstract.para: Once &kdump; has captured a vmcore file, use the crash utility to inspect it and find out what the kernel was doing at the moment it panicked.

step.para: Enable the product's Debug repository. It is disabled by default. List your repositories to find its exact alias, then enable it:
step.screen: &prompt.sudo; zypper lr | grep -i debug &prompt.sudo; zypper modifyrepo --enable DEBUG_REPO_ALIAS

step.para: Install crash and the debuginfo package of the running kernel. The package name contains the kernel flavor, the last part of the uname -r output. For the default flavor, this is kernel-default-debuginfo. The following command inserts the flavor automatically:

note.title: The debuginfo package version must match the running kernel exactly
note.para: If the debuginfo package installs a version newer than the kernel you crashed (for example, because an update arrived after the crash but before you reboot), crash refuses to load it with a version mismatch error. Reboot onto the newest installed kernel first, and confirm uname -r matches the Kernel version line in the crash directory's README.txt before proceeding.

step.para: The debuginfo package alone is not enough: On &productnameshort;, its vmlinux.debug file contains only debug symbols, not the actual kernel code and data crash needs alongside them. Place the real kernel image from the matching kernel package next to vmlinux.debug. step.remark: ssarkar: the per-architecture layout is from the kernel-default and kernel-default-debuginfo package file lists (6.12.0-160000.26.1) and the SL-16.1 kernel spec: vmlinux.xz on x86-64, AArch64 and IBM Z, uncompressed vmlinux and no vmlinux.xz on POWER, vmlinux.debug in /usr/lib/debug/usr/lib/modules/VERSION/ on all of them. The cp variant was not run on POWER. The kernel built for the NVIDIA product (SL-16.1-NV branch) has the flavor nvidia64kb, hence the flavor-independent debuginfo package name.

section.title: Opening the vmcore file in crash
section.para: Start crash, giving it the kernel image you just placed and the captured vmcore file:
Sample output, from a crash deliberately triggered as described in :
section.screen: KERNEL: /usr/lib/debug/usr/lib/modules/6.12.0-160000.37-default/vmlinux DEBUGINFO: /usr/lib/debug/usr/lib/modules/6.12.0-160000.37-default//vmlinux.debug DUMPFILE: /var/crash/2026-09-10-11-33/vmcore [PARTIAL DUMP] CPUS: 2 DATE: Thu Sep 10 11:33:30 CEST 2026 UPTIME: 00:00:57 LOAD AVERAGE: 0.25, 0.08, 0.03 TASKS: 173 NODENAME: sles16 RELEASE: 6.12.0-160000.37-default VERSION: #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Aug 6 15:43:26 UTC 2026 (cf8ec7a) MACHINE: x86_64 (2304 Mhz) MEMORY: 4 GB PANIC: "Kernel panic - not syncing: sysrq triggered crash" PID: 4400 COMMAND: "tee" TASK: ffff8e020581c080 [THREAD_INFO: ffff8e020581c080] CPU: 0 STATE: TASK_RUNNING (PANIC) crash> bt PID: 4400 TASK: ffff8e020581c080 CPU: 0 COMMAND: "tee" #0 [ffffd3de00e17928] machine_kexec at ffffffff94a95552 #1 [ffffd3de00e17988] __crash_kexec at ffffffff94bd61eb #2 [ffffd3de00e17a48] panic at ffffffff9572c8fd #3 [ffffd3de00e17ac8] sysrq_handle_crash at ffffffff9529e89a #4 [ffffd3de00e17ad0] __handle_sysrq.cold at ffffffff9576a328 #5 [ffffd3de00e17b00] write_sysrq_trigger at ffffffff9529f439 #6 [ffffd3de00e17b28] proc_reg_write at ffffffff94f0db9a #7 [ffffd3de00e17b40] vfs_write at ffffffff94e5c99b #8 [ffffd3de00e17bd8] ksys_write at ffffffff94e5d017 #9 [ffffd3de00e17c10] do_syscall_64 at ffffffff9578a94d #10 [ffffd3de00e17f40] entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe at ffffffff9580012f RIP: 00007f4a1a86f514 RSP: 00007ffe6cfa0538 RFLAGS: 00000202 RAX: ffffffffffffffda RBX: 0000000000000002 RCX: 00007f4a1a86f514 RDX: 0000000000000002 RSI: 00007ffe6cfa06b0 RDI: 0000000000000003 RBP: 00007ffe6cfa06b0 R8: 0000000000000004 R9: 0000000000000001 R10: 00000000000001b6 R11: 0000000000000202 R12: 0000000000000002 R13: 000055aa042a22c0 R14: 00007f4a1a950ea0 R15: 0000000000000001 ORIG_RAX: 0000000000000001 CS: 0033 SS: 002b crash> quit

callout.para: The process that happened to be running when the crash was triggered, not necessarily a sign of a problem with that process. Here it is tee because the crash in this example was deliberately triggered with echo c | sudo tee /proc/sysrq-trigger. On a real, unplanned crash this would show whatever command was running at the time.

section.para: The banner shows the panic reason, the running process and basic system information. bt without arguments shows the call stack of the process active at the moment of the crash, here showing the path from the sysrq-trigger write down to machine_kexec, which is &kexec; handing control to the capture kernel.

section.title: Useful follow-up commands

listitem.para: Lists the processes that were running at the moment of the crash.
Resolves a kernel symbol to its address, or an address back to a symbol.
Lists the open file descriptors of the current process.

section.para: crash has extensive built-in help: Run help COMMAND inside a session for details on any of these.
